_doc: Single source for SD-94's technology choices; see SD-08/stack.json for the format. `how` is spoken, so it carries no code; keep summary cells under 36 characters.

stack.heading: Rule store: PostgreSQL with a counter row
stack.title: One place that is strictly correct: it assigns the version order
stack.pick: PostgreSQL, one primary, a synchronous standby, a counter row per list
stack.why: The only part that must give one total order. Fifty changes a second is tiny for it; the risk is the commit-order race, not throughput.
stack.how: Each change is a transaction that locks the list's counter row, increments it and stamps the change with the new version. Because the row lock is taken before the commit, version order equals commit order. Every change is also appended to an audit table, with who, why and the approval.
stack.detail: Per-key versions let a merge be idempotent and independent of arrival order.
rejected: A replicated log as the primary store
More machinery than fifty writes a second needs, and the order is still decided by one leader.
An eventually consistent store
It cannot give one order, which is the one thing this store is for.
drill: Two operators publish at the same moment. How is the order of their changes decided?
Both transactions lock the list's counter row, so one waits. The version number is taken under the lock, so version order is commit order. The trap is stamping the version before the commit.
the counter row lock; version taken under it

stack.heading: Compiler: snapshots, deltas, a digest chain
stack.title: A job that turns the list into immutable, verifiable artifacts
stack.pick: A Go job: a snapshot every N versions, a delta per version, a manifest, a digest chain
stack.why: Every tier can cache an immutable artifact for ever, and every node can verify it before it applies it.
stack.how: On each new version the compiler writes a delta from the previous one, content-addressed by its hash. Every hundredth version it writes a full snapshot. A tiny manifest names the latest version, its digest and the previous digest, so the artifacts form a chain. A node that is behind by less than the delta window applies deltas, and otherwise fetches a snapshot.
stack.detail: Snapshots are compact and sorted, so a node can load them without rebuilding.
rejected: A full file on a timer
Four terabytes a push, and no integrity check.
Per-request lookups only
The list service joins every request's availability.
drill: A node was offline for a day. How does it catch up, and how does it know the result is right?

It reads the manifest, sees it is behind by more than the delta window, fetches the latest snapshot, then applies deltas. The digest chain proves the artifacts form a sequence and the digest proves the result.
manifest; snapshot plus deltas; chain and digest

stack.heading: Origin and relay tree: object storage and HTTP caches
stack.title: Object storage behind a tree of caching relays
stack.pick: Object storage as origin; regional, then zone, HTTP caching relays
stack.why: Immutable, content-addressed files are exactly what object storage and an HTTP cache do well. Five hundred nodes cost one origin fetch.
stack.how: Artifacts sit in object storage with names that include their hash. Regional relays, then zone relays, cache them with a very long lifetime. The manifest is the one mutable object, about a hundred bytes, cached for a second or two. Nodes poll the manifest and also accept a push hint, so a change lands in seconds.
stack.detail: Manifest age at the node is a metric: a stale manifest is harmless to correctness and exactly how a ban fails to land.
rejected: Pub-sub as the only path
A missed message is never repaired, and there is no catch-up.
A configuration fabric we already run
Adopt it for transport, and keep our compiler, gates and audit.
summary: Cache for ever; one origin fetch

stack.heading: Enforcement agent: a library with a local set
stack.title: A library in the serving process: local set, atomic swap, no network
stack.pick: Library in the server, a compact local filter with an exact tier behind it
stack.why: The check is on every request, so it cannot wait for a network call. The local copy answers, and it is swapped atomically, never edited in place.
stack.how: The agent loads the artifact into a new in-memory set, verifies the digest, then swaps one pointer. Check reads the current pointer and never blocks on a swap. A compact filter answers about ninety-nine percent of requests with a definite not listed. A maybe goes to the exact lookup tier through a small cache.
stack.detail: If the control plane is unreachable the node keeps its last good set, and a bound says how stale it may become.
rejected: A network lookup per request
The list service becomes part of every request's availability.
Editing the set in place
A reader can see a half-applied update.
drill: The agent applies a corrupt artifact. What does the serving process see?
Nothing: the digest check fails before the swap, the node keeps the last good set and reports the failure. The trap is verifying after applying.
verify the digest before the swap; keep the last good set

stack.heading: Control plane: stages, gates and a kill flag
stack.title: Treat the list like code: stages, a gate, a kill flag
stack.pick: Go service, etcd for fleet state, staged rollout by percentage
stack.why: A bad list is everywhere in seconds unless something can stop it. A staged rollout with a gate buys the minutes a person needs.
stack.how: A new version is staged to one percent of nodes, then ten, then everyone, with a gate between stages that watches the rejection rate and the error rate. A kill flag halts the rollout and holds every node at its current version. Fleet state, meaning which node runs which version, lives in etcd.
stack.detail: A node never depends on the control plane to enforce; it depends on it only to move.
rejected: Fan out to the whole fleet at once
One mistyped line is a global outage in twenty seconds.
Gate by a human approval only
The gate is a minutes-long human step; automated metrics catch the first ten seconds.
summary: Fan out at once; human gate
Minutes to stop a bad list
drill: An operator types slash eight instead of slash twenty-eight. What limits the damage?
The one percent stage: the gate sees the rejection rate jump and halts the rollout before the next stage. The kill flag freezes the rest. The trap is relying on the reviewer.
the staged gate; the kill flag

stack.heading: Policy tool: review and explain
stack.title: A web app that publishes, approves and explains
stack.pick: Web app and Go API, two-person approval, an explain view
stack.why: People change the list under pressure. The tool makes a risky change need a second person and makes any verdict explainable afterwards.
stack.how: Changes are drafted, diffed against the live list, and approved by a second person when they match more than a threshold. The explain view answers why a key was or was not blocked: which rule, which version, who added it and why. Every action lands in the audit table.
stack.detail: A dry run shows the matched count before anything publishes.
rejected: Direct database edits
No diff, no second person, no audit trail.
A spreadsheet upload
No validation of a typed range, and no explanation afterwards.

1: a missed message is never repaired; polling the manifest catches up.
2: arrival order is not intent order; per-key versions make the merge idempotent.
3: Fanning out to the whole fleet at once
one mistyped line is global in seconds; stages and a gate bound it.
4: Making the control plane a dependency of enforcement
its outage would stop enforcement; nodes keep the last good set within a bound.
5: The full list in every node's memory
it does not fit; a filter in front and an exact tier behind do.
6: Calling a slow external source on every request
its latency becomes ours; prefer a bulk list, else a bounded cache and a budget.
7: the fleet can be green while a ban never lands; probe from change to enforcement.
